intro:
**The City That Persecuted Its Noblest Citizen**

The historical context of al-Balad reflects the bitter paradox of Makkah. The Quraysh boasted of their city as an inviolable sanctuary of peace (*ḥaramun āmin*), where shedding blood and hunting animals were strictly forbidden; yet within that very sanctuary, they felt completely free to brutalize, torture, and plot the murder of their noblest citizen, the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ! Verse 2 carries a biting irony: *“And you are free of restriction / a dweller in this city”*—meaning the Quraysh have made your blood lawful in the very city they proclaim sacred. And, the sūrah addresses the arrogant oligarch (such as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah or Abū Jahl) who boasted: *“I have spent wealth in vast abundance!”* (90:6). Sūrah al-Balad asks him: *“Does he think that no one sees him?”* (90:7).

**The Structural Architecture and the Steep Ascent**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Balad moves across three distinct movements:

1. The Gifts of Perception and the Two Highways (8–10): Directs man to his biological and moral architecture: *“Have We not made for him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips, and guided him to the two highways [of good and evil]?”* (90:8–10).

3. Conquering the Steep Ascent: Al-ʿAqabah (11–20): Delivers the dramatic challenge of human ethics: *“But he has not broken through the steep path (*fa-lā iqtaḥama al-ʿaqabah*)! And what can make you know what is the steep path?”* Verses 13–16 define this uphill climb: - *Fakku raqabah*: The emancipation of a slave from bondage. - *Feeding on a day of severe hunger (*fī yawmin dhī masghabah*):* - An orphan of near relationship (*yatīman dhā maqrabah*), - Or an impoverished person lying in the dust (*miskīnan dhā matrabah*). It defines the community of the summit in verse 17: those who believe and enjoin one another to patient endurance (*al-ṣabr*) and enjoin one another to mercy (*al-marḥamah*). They are the *Companions of the Right* (*Aṣḥāb al-Maymanah*), while those who deny divine signs are the *Companions of the Left*, enclosed by a vault of fire (*nārun mu'ṣadah*).

It opens with an intimate, solemn oath sworn by the sacred city of Makkah and the physical presence of the Prophet within its precincts: *“I swear by this city [Makkah], and you, [O Muḥammad], are a free resident of this city, and by the begetter and that which he begot—We have certainly created man into hardship/struggle (*fī kabad*)!”* (90:1–4).

verses.1:
> I do swear by this city ˹of Mecca˺—

**An Oath Lifts a Place Above Itself**

An Arabic oath is an instrument of weight. The speaker swears by whatever is heaviest in the mind of the listener, and the weight of the thing sworn by carries across into the sentence sworn for. When revelation swears by a city, it declares that the city stands in God's reckoning and not merely in the reckoning of caravans. Mecca is identified here without being named: *bi-hādhā al-balad*, "by this city", with no proper noun attached. For the first audience the reference was never ambiguous, since only one place in their world answered to the definite article, yet the choice of the common noun keeps the object double. It is a settled place in the general sense, and it is the exact ground under the hearers' feet. The same gesture recurs twice more. Mecca closes the oath list of 95:1–3 as "this secure city ˹of Mecca˺" (95:3), and the command that grounds the Prophet's mission in geography reads: "I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city ˹of Mecca˺, Who has made it sacred" (27:91). Sanctity is a property of the place, and the oath is one way of saying so out loud.

The early exegetes read the opening as more than an oath. Mujāhid, in the report Khusayf carries from him, took the particle *lā* standing before *uqsimu* as a refusal aimed at the Quraysh first and an oath second: the "nay" rebuts them, and only then does the sentence swear by the city. On that reading the verse contradicts a claim its audience was already making before it swears by anything at all. The city itself was never in doubt. Shabīb bin Bishr transmits from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʻAbbas, that "this city" means Makkah, and the identification is recorded as the settled sense of the words rather than as one opinion among several.

**Sacred Because of What Stands Inside It**

A city has no sanctity of its own. Mecca is honoured for the House it holds, and the revelation says this directly: "Surely the first House ˹of worship˺ established for humanity is the one at Bakkah—a blessed sanctuary and a guide for ˹all˺ people" (3:96). The sanctity is derivative, and it is old. Abraham and Ishmael were given the task of purifying that House "for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺" (2:125), and Abraham had earlier settled part of his family "in a barren valley, near Your Sacred House" (14:37). None of this describes fertile land or a strategic harbour. The valley was dry, and the city's claim on reverence rests completely on worship. That matters for the oath in front of us. Swearing by Mecca is not swearing by prosperity or by tribal prestige; it is swearing by the fact that God placed a House in a waterless valley and made the place holy on that account. Every later claim Mecca's residents make about their own status has to be measured against that origin.

Ibn Kathīr's framing of the oath adds two things the bare wording does not give. He names Makkah the Mother of the Towns, the title the revelation itself uses when it sets the city's warning against everything surrounding it (42:7 — *“so you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it”*). And he reads the oath as a summons to attention rather than as ornament: God swears by the city and addresses its resident in the same breath, in order to draw out the weight of its sanctity at the very moment its people are themselves in a state of sanctity. The honour and the obligation are therefore announced together, which is the structure the rest of the chapter keeps.

**A Sanctuary That Obligates Its Residents**

Abraham's own prayer for this place asked for two things: "make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day" (2:126). Security and provision were requested as conditions for worship, and the answer included a warning for the ungrateful within the same verse. Mecca's status is repeatedly described in these terms elsewhere: God "fed them against hunger and made them secure against fear" (106:4), and the safe haven is set against the surrounding lands where "people ˹all˺ around them are snatched away" (29:67). The residents therefore live inside a favour, not inside an exemption. The oath of this verse invokes the honoured status of the city in a sūrah that goes on to interrogate the people who benefit from it, and that contrast is the first cut the sūrah makes. To be sworn by is to be held. A place that God dignifies with an oath has residents whose conduct is now under the same oath, and the privilege of living in the sanctuary carries a debt that residence alone does not discharge.
verses.2:
> even though you ˹O Prophet˺ are subject to abuse in this city—

**A Parenthesis Inside a Solemn Sentence**

The oath is interrupted before it finishes. Between the swearing by the city and the swearing by parent and child, a clause is inserted about the Prophet's own situation in that city. Arabic allows this kind of parenthetical, and the interruption is the point: the city has just been honoured with an oath, and the very next breath records how the city treats its most honoured resident. The grammar of the clause is compressed. The key word is *ḥill*, a verbal noun that can mean either "one who is permitted, for whom something has become lawful" or "one who is residing, alighting, present in a place". Both senses are live in the classical language, and the choice between them decides whether the verse is a promise of military permission or a statement of honourable residence. Exegetes have taken both, and the tradition leans heavily toward the first.

**The Verified Rule About Fighting in the Sanctuary**

The claim that the Prophet alone was permitted what others were not is not an inference of the commentators; it is his own statement, delivered on the day of the conquest. Ibn ʿAbbās reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has made Mecca a sanctuary since the day He created the heavens and the earth, and it will remain a sanctuary by virtue of the sanctity Allah has bestowed upon it till the Day of Resurrection. Fighting in it was not made lawful for anyone before me, nor will it be made lawful for anyone after me, and it was not made lawful for me except for a short period of time" (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3189). The same report is transmitted in the Book of Sales with the added detail that its thorny bushes may not be uprooted and its game may not be chased (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2090). Two things follow. The exception is personal, not general: it belongs to one man and to one hour, and it establishes no precedent for anyone after him. And the exception is short, which means the sanctuary's rule survives intact even in the moment it is set aside.

The permission is not the commentators' inference from the grammar. Ibn ʻAbbas states it as a direct address — "O Muhammad, it is permissible for you to fight in it" — and the same reading is recorded from Saʿid bin Jubayr, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿAṭiyyah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, as-Suddī and Ibn Zayd. Al-Hasan al-Basri fixed its length: Allah made it lawful for him for one hour of a day, which is the measure the agreed-upon report gives. That report also carries a second wording, aimed at anyone who would generalise the exception: if a man uses the Messenger's fighting there as his excuse, he is to be told that Allah permitted it for His Messenger and has not permitted it for him. The clause in the oath is therefore not a hint. It is a ruling with a named owner and an expiry.

**The Irony the Clause Records**

Whatever reading is preferred, the clause carries a rebuke aimed at the city's custodians. The Quraysh held the keys of the Kaʿbah and drew their prestige from the House. The verse places inside the oath a fact that dismantles the claim from within — the sanctuary's own keepers were abusing the man whom God had sent to them, in the city whose holiness they administered. Sanctity of place did not produce reverence in its inhabitants. The pattern is not unique to Mecca, and the Qur'an states it as a general principle where it asks how a safe haven can coexist with ingratitude: "Have they not seen how We have made ˹Mecca˺ a safe haven, whereas people ˹all˺ around them are snatched away? How can they then believe in falsehood and deny Allah's favours?" (29:67).
verses.3:
> and by every parent and ˹their˺ child

**Why the Second Term Uses "What" Rather Than "Who"**

The pairing is asymmetric in Arabic, and the asymmetry is meaningful. The first half is a definite noun, *al-wālid*, the begetter, a person with an identity. The second half is introduced by *mā*, the relative that ordinarily covers non-personal things, "that which he begot". Grammarians and exegetes have read that particle in two ways. It can be an indefinite covering a plurality, "and his offspring", which keeps the second term personal while refusing to give it a single shape; or it can mark the begetting itself, the act and its product considered together. The indefinite form does real work. Had the verse said "and his child", the oath would have named one relation and left the rest outside. By saying "that which he begot", it sweeps in every generation, every descendant, and every link in a chain that no one can count. There is also a rhetorical economy in the choice. The pair is stated at maximum generality so that no listener can stand outside it. Every hearer is somebody's child, and almost every hearer is somebody's parent. The oath closes over the audience completely, which is what an oath at the head of a sūrah is meant to do before it says something unwelcome.

**Generation as the Deepest Human Bond**

Swearing by parent and child puts the strongest bond human beings know at the centre of the argument. That bond is not chosen. It is given, it precedes consent, and it carries obligations that no contract creates. The Qur'an builds large parts of its ethics on it: honour to parents sits next to worship of God in the covenant taken from the children of Israel, "be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy" (2:83). The decree of the later revelation is starker still, "never say to them ˹even˺ ‘ugh,’ nor yell at them" (17:23). Lineage also organises human societies, and nowhere more visibly than in the city this sūrah swears by, where a man's standing followed from whose son he was. To make that bond the object of a divine oath is to take it seriously on its own terms and then to place it under God's authority. The bond is real, and it is not ultimate.

Placing parent and child under an oath removes the possibility of treating descent as a shield. "Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you" (49:13).

**Who the Begetter Is**

The grammar fixes the shape of the oath; the exegetes settle who stands inside it. A long list of the early authorities took the pair as Adam and his children: Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Sufyān ath-Thawrī, Saʿid bin Jubayr, as-Suddī, al-Ḥasan al-Basri, Khusayf and Shurahbil bin Saʿd. Ibn Kathīr calls the choice good and strong, and his reason is structural. The oath swears first by the Mother of the Towns, which is a dwelling, and then by those who dwell in it — the father of mankind and his descendants. Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī took the pair more narrowly, as Ibrāhīm and his progeny, a reading both Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim preserve. Ibn Jarīr himself preferred the widest sense of all: every father and every child. The three readings narrow and widen one bond, and none of them leaves a hearer outside. The first makes the oath about the whole race, the second about the line that raised the House this sūrah swears by, and the third about the family standing in the room.
verses.4:
> Indeed, We have created humankind in ˹constant˺ struggle

**The Statement the Oath Was Taken For**

After two oaths the sūrah delivers what was sworn to, and it is a single sentence about the human condition. Humanity was created *fī kabad*, in struggle. The word is the pivot of the whole chapter. *Kabad* carries the sense of toil, strain and difficulty, and it is set here as a created feature rather than an accident. Human beings are not placed in struggle as a punishment added later; they are constituted in it. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's gloss, preserved in the early commentaries, states the two halves of the cost: the hardships of this world in life and the severities of the Hereafter after it.

**Three Readings of Kabad, and Which Holds**

The interpretive tradition offers three distinct accounts of the word. The second narrows it to the physical sequence of human existence, connecting the verse to "His mother carried him ˹in hardship˺ and delivered him ˹in hardship˺" (46:15), and reading the struggle as the stages that follow — weaning, teething, earning a living, ageing, dying.

Two of the three accounts are recorded from the Companions and their students, and both are physical. Ibn ʻAbbas, in the report ʿAṭāʾ passed on through Ibn Abī Najīḥ and Jurayj, said that man was created while in hardship, and then asked: do you not see him? He pointed at birth and at the cutting of the teeth as the first instalments of the struggle. Mujāhid set the same sequence out from its beginning — a drop of sperm, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, endured at every step — which is the order the revelation uses as its proof of power (22:5 — *“We did create you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then ˹developed you into˺ a clinging clot ˹of blood˺, then a lump of flesh”*). He tied it to the mother's hardship cited above and added the two burdens that come after it: she breastfeeds him with hardship, and his livelihood is a hardship.

The third reading carries the struggle forward into a whole life. Saʿid bin Jubayr glossed the word as hardship and the seeking of a livelihood; ʿIkrimah as hardship and long-suffering; Qatādah, simply, as difficulty. These are the readings the rest of the sūrah runs on, because the verses that follow are not about birth but about spending, feeding and refusing, and they need a struggle a grown man is still standing inside. Al-Hasan's version, given above, states it in both halves at once: the hardships of this world in life, and the severities of the Hereafter after it.

**Struggle as the Setting for Choice**

A condition of constant difficulty is not a defect in the design; it is the condition under which choice becomes visible. Ease hides preference. When nothing costs anything, a person's decisions reveal nothing about him. Difficulty forces the question every time: what will you give up, and for whom? The Qur'an states the same logic where it asks, "Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you?" (2:214), and it describes the testing as so severe that even a messenger cries out for help.

**Why Toil Is Not the Whole Truth About the Human Being**

The same sūrah that calls humanity created in struggle also honours it in the verses that follow, and the two claims have to be held together. Toil is the condition; dignity is the endowment. Elsewhere the revelation states the honour side of the account: "Indeed, We have dignified the children of Adam, carried them on land and sea, granted them good and lawful provisions, and privileged them far above many of Our creatures" (17:70). A creature made in the best form is also a creature made to labour, and neither statement cancels the other. The pairing is what makes the human case distinctive. Animals labour and do not know why; angels know and do not labour. The human being does both, and the strain is the price of the knowing. Read against that background, *kabad* is not a slur on humanity. It is a description of the only creature whose effort can be morally significant, because only a creature that resists something can be said to have chosen it.
verses.5:
> Do they think that no one has power over them

**A Question That Exposes an Assumption**

The sūrah turns from statement to interrogation, and the interrogation is aimed at a belief rather than at an act. *A-yaḥsabu a lan yaqdira ʿalayhi aḥad* — does he reckon that no one will ever have power over him? The question is not asked for information. It is asked to drag a private assumption into the open where it can be examined. The assumption is the real offence; the spending and the boasting that follow are only its symptoms. The form of the question does precise work. A yes-or-no question about a belief forces the hearer to inspect a belief he has probably never stated, and probably would not state if asked directly. Nobody says out loud, "no one can overpower me". People simply act as though it were true, and the acting is what the verse targets. The shift from "humankind" in the previous verse to "he" here is deliberate too: a general condition is now being lived out in a particular temperament, and the reader is invited to recognise the temperament in himself before he recognises it in anyone else.

The earliest glosses read the question as being about the wealth rather than about the man. Al-Hasan al-Basri took it to mean that no one is able to take his wealth: the power the boaster doubts is the power to reach what he owns. Qatādah read it further, as a denial of the audit — the son of Adam thinks he will not be asked about this wealth of his, how he earned it and how he spent it. Both glosses keep the question welded to the boast that follows, and both make that boast its own proof: the man announces the sum he destroyed because he assumes the sum will never be itemised. The interrogation Qatādah describes is given in full under the verse that asks whether anyone sees him (90:7).

**Wealth as the Evidence for Immunity**

The belief the question exposes has a material basis. In a mercantile city, a man's security was purchased: allies bought, debts owed to him, dependants who needed his protection, and a store of wealth that answered every demand before it arrived. Money converts into influence, influence converts into immunity, and immunity feels like permanence. The Qur'an treats this chain as the standard mechanism of delusion, and it names the mechanism wherever it appears. Wealth and children are described repeatedly as a test rather than as a possession: "And know that your wealth and your children are only a test and that with Allah is a great reward" (8:28), and again "Your wealth and children are only a test" (64:15). The verse about competition is blunter still: "Competition for more ˹gains˺ diverts you ˹from Allah˺" (102:1). What the boaster mistakes for a fortress is, on the revelation's account, an examination paper. The error is not that he values wealth; it is that he reads wealth as a verdict about his own standing, and then infers from the verdict that he cannot be reached.
verses.6:
> boasting, “I have wasted enormous wealth!”

**Why Regret Nullifies the Gift**

The Qur'an has a precise doctrine on this point, and it is stated in commercial language. Charity followed by reminders and hurtful words is compared to "a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain— leaving it just a bare stone", and the verdict is that "such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity" (2:264). The image is agricultural and exact: the soil that looks fertile is only a film, and the first heavy rain washes it off to show the rock beneath. A gift given with a running commentary on its cost is that rock. The contrast verse describes the other case: "The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains" (2:261). Multiplication belongs to the gift that is released without a ledger attached. The boaster of this verse has inverted the arithmetic. He has paid the price of giving and forfeited its return, and the verse he is quoted in exists to tell him so in his own words.

**Wealth as a Stewardship, Not a Possession**

Underneath the complaint is a false premise about ownership. The man speaks of his wealth as something that has been taken from him, which assumes that it was his in an absolute sense. The revelation does not grant that assumption. Wealth is repeatedly described as provision from God rather than as an acquisition: "O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth" (2:267), where both halves of the property — earnings and produce — are attributed to divine provision. The test language makes the same point from the other direction: "Your wealth and children are only a test, but Allah ˹alone˺ has a great reward" (64:15). Something held on trust cannot be said to be wasted when it is spent on the terms of the trust. The boaster's error is therefore not stinginess alone. It is a misdescription of his own position. He is a trustee accounting to himself as though he were an owner who has been robbed, and the misdescription is what makes his generosity feel like plunder to him.

**The Boast as a Social Performance**

The speech is public, and its audience matters. A man who announces how much he has destroyed is performing for other men: look at what my standing costs, look at what I can afford to lose. In a city where rank was measured by expenditure, the announcement buys status even as it protests the expense. The Qur'an names this mechanism in a single phrase when it calls worldly life "play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children" (57:20), and it warns that the competition diverts before the reckoning arrives: "Then, on that Day, you will definitely be questioned about ˹your worldly˺ pleasures" (102:8). The performance has a cost the performer does not see. He is buying the applause of people who cannot pay him, at the price of a reward that could have been settled in full. The verse captures the whole transaction in five words, which is why it is quoted rather than paraphrased. Nothing needs to be added to a sentence that convicts itself.

**The Verb the Boaster Chose**

The wording of the boast repays a moment's attention, because the early commentators read it as a statement of quantity rather than of loss. Ibn Kathīr takes the line to mean that the son of Adam says, "I spent an abundance of wealth", and he gives that sense from Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī among others. The verb the man actually uses is a verb of ruin — *ahlaktu*, I have destroyed — and the word beside it is one of massing, wealth heaped on wealth. The sentence therefore carries its contradiction inside its own grammar. He describes generosity in the vocabulary of damage, and he gives the amount in the tone of a man reading out an injury done to him. That is why the sūrah quotes him instead of describing him: the boast is already a confession.

**What the Verse Is Not Saying**

The condemnation here is not a condemnation of spending. The sūrah goes on to define the good in expenditure — freeing a person, feeding the hungry in a famine — and the Qur'an elsewhere praises those "who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly" (2:274). Large gifts are not the problem; the sūrah asks for them. The problem is the inner accounting that accompanies this man's gift. He measures the giving in loss, and a gift measured in loss is not really a gift but a purchase, with the seller being other people's opinion.
verses.7:
> Do they think that no one sees them

**Sight Added to Power**

Two questions stand together in this passage, and the pairing is deliberate. The first asked whether he reckons that no one will ever have power over him; this one asks whether he reckons that no one sees him. Power and sight are the two faculties whose absence would make wrongdoing safe. If no one can act on you, you cannot be stopped; if no one sees you, you cannot be charged. A man who believes both has constructed a world in which his conduct has no consequences at all, and the two questions dismantle that world one plank at a time.

**The Recurring Formula of Divine Seeing**

The Qur'an returns to this question in a form so close that it reads as a refrain. Of the man who drags another to prevent him from praying, the text asks: "Does he not know that Allah sees ˹all˺?" (96:14). The accountability of the senses is stated outright elsewhere: "Do not follow what you have no ˹sure˺ knowledge of. Indeed, all will be called to account for ˹their˺ hearing, sight, and intellect" (17:36). In the legislation on charity the same assurance appears with commercial precision: "Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah" (2:270), and "And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do" (2:265). None of these statements is offered as consolation. They are offered as the closing term of an argument about conduct. Once a person accepts that his acts are seen, the calculation he has been running collapses, because the calculation assumed an audience of other people only.

The "anyone" of the question has a name in the earliest glosses. Mujāhid read it as Allah: does he think that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not see him? Others among the Salaf said the same. The point is small and it closes a gap. A man can believe that people are not watching without believing that God is not, and the verse allows him no such middle position. The witness who matters is not in the room, and the seeing the question denies is the seeing that reaches the motive as well as the act.

**What the Wealth Will Be Asked About**

The tradition specifies the interrogation this verse implies. A report transmitted from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd in Sunan al-Tirmidhī — al-Tirmidhī himself called the tradition *gharīb*, unusual in its chain — states that on the Day of Resurrection the feet of the son of Adam will not move until he has been questioned about five matters: on what he spent his life, in what he let his youth pass, from which he acquired his property, on what he spent it, and what he did with what he knew. Two of the five are financial, and both concern the same sum of money from two directions: where it came from and where it went. That is exactly the boaster's exposure. He announced the amount he had destroyed; the report says he will be asked how he obtained it. The verse in front of us is the short form of the same warning, and it is why the question about being seen follows the boast about spending rather than some other act.

**Seeing the Motive Behind the Gift**

Observation reaches further than the act. A person can perform a generous deed and still fail, because what is seen includes the intention underneath. The revelation states the rule in agricultural terms: charity followed by reminders and hurtful words is "a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain— leaving it just a bare stone", and "such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity" (2:264). The boaster of the previous verse is precisely this case. He gave, and he resented giving, and he advertised the cost of it. Nothing about the transfer of money was hidden, and nothing about the resentment was visible to the recipients. The verse about being seen addresses the second fact. The witnesses who applauded the gift cannot see the complaint running underneath it, and the One who is asked about is not limited to what they see. This is the sharpest edge of the question, and it is why the verse is phrased as a question rather than as a statement.
verses.8:
> Have We not given them two eyes

**Why Sight Is Named First**

Of all the faculties, sight is the one on which most human knowledge depends, and the revelation consistently names it first when it enumerates what God has given. "And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing, and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect so perhaps you would be thankful" (16:78). The order in that verse is instructive: the newborn knows nothing, and the first endowments are the instruments of knowing. The same triad appears in the command to speak about the gift: "He is the One Who brought you into being and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect. ˹Yet˺ you hardly give any thanks" (67:23). Sight comes at the head of this sūrah's list because it is the sense through which the world becomes evidence. A man who has never seen a mountain, a starving child, or another man's face has not merely lost data; he has lost the raw material from which moral judgements are made. To give eyes is to make a person capable of being addressed by what he sees.

**The Sense Most Easily Abused**

Sight is also the faculty most exposed to misuse, and the sūrah knows it. The eye can be directed or averted. A man walking past a starving relative can see him, or can manage not to. The Qur'an's moral vocabulary for this is exact: the ones who "repulse the orphan" (107:2) are not blind to him; they have seen him and refused. The connection to this verse is the reason the faculties are listed at all. God has not given eyes to make the receiver comfortable; He has given them so that the world can present its claims. Every faculty listed here has a corresponding obligation, and the obligation of the eye is attention. A person who has been given the capacity to notice and chooses not to has converted a gift into an offence, and the verse's question form — have We not made for him two eyes? — is the first step in charging him with it.
verses.9:
> a tongue, and two lips

**Speech Completes the Equipment**

The list of endowments moves from receiving to producing. Eyes take the world in; a tongue puts something out into it. The sūrah adds speech to sight without comment, and the addition is the largest of the four items, because speech is what makes a human being an agent among other agents rather than a spectator. The revelation treats speech as a direct gift rather than as a biological by-product: among the mercies enumerated in the sūrah of the Merciful is that God created humanity and "taught them speech" (55:4). The pairing with creation in that verse is significant. Speech is not described as something human beings developed but as something they were taught, which places it in the same category as the eyes and lips named here. Every item in this list is presented as received, and the receiver has no claim to have earned any of it. Completing the equipment is what the verse is doing, and the completion matters because the earlier items were passive. A reader who has been given eyes and a heart has been fitted out; the addition of speech makes him an agent, and the agency is what the chapter's commands assume.

**One Small Organ With Unlimited Reach**

The tongue is the smallest of the instruments named and by far the most consequential. The Qur'an states the accountability of speech in a single line that leaves no room for exceptions: "not a word does a person utter without having a ˹vigilant˺ observer ready ˹to write it down˺" (50:18).

**Two Lips as the Gate**

The sūrah does not stop at the tongue. It adds two lips, and the addition is not anatomical padding. Lips are the gate of speech: they shape sound into language, and they can also close. A tongue without lips produces noise; lips without a tongue produce silence. The pairing names both capacities in one breath, which is to say that the gift includes the power of restraint. Every faculty in this list has been given with its own limit built in — eyes that can be lowered, a tongue that can be held — and the limit is part of the gift rather than a restriction on it. The Qur'an legislates the same principle where it commands believing men "to lower their gaze and guard their chastity", adding "That is purer for them" (24:30). Control of the instrument is presented as the condition of its proper use, and the two lips are the physical sign of that condition in the organ of speech. The tongue's power is set out at length in the sūrah that opens with a curse on its misuse: "Woe to every backbiter, slanderer, who amasses wealth ˹greedily˺ and counts it ˹repeatedly˺, thinking that their wealth will make them immortal!" (104:1–3). The conjunction is not accidental.

The early glosses give the two lips three jobs, and only one of them is speech. They help a man to speak, to eat his food, and to give his face and mouth their form. The middle item is the one this sūrah goes on to need. The same organ that gates a word is the organ that takes in a mouthful, and the whole middle of the chapter is about whether a mouthful was handed to somebody else. A reader who takes the lips only as the door of speech has read half the gift. They are also the instrument of eating, which is why the demand that follows — feed the orphaned relative on a day of famine — is addressed to a body that has already been told what its mouth is for.
verses.10:
> and shown them the two ways ˹of right and wrong˺

**The Fourth Item Is Not an Organ**

Three instruments are listed, and then a fourth gift of a different kind. Eyes, a tongue and two lips are parts of a body; the two ways are not. After endowing the human being with the capacity to perceive and to speak, the sūrah records that he was shown where to go. The shift is the hinge of the chapter's opening argument. Equipment without direction produces a creature who can act and cannot choose, and the choice is what the rest of the sūrah is about. The verse therefore completes an account that began with the body: here is what you were given to see with, to speak with, and here is what you were shown.

**Najdayn: The Two High Roads**

The Arabic word is *najdayn*, the dual of *najd*, which means an elevated tract and, by extension, a road that runs across high ground and is visible from a distance. The dual form is precise: not many roads, but two. Arabic usage supports the sense of a clear, well-marked route rather than a vague direction, and the Qur'an's own parallel confirms it. Speaking of the same human being, the revelation says: "We already showed them the Way, whether they ˹choose to˺ be grateful or ungrateful" (76:3). The showing is stated as a completed act, and the two outcomes are named as options rather than as destinations already assigned. A second parallel describes the same endowment from the inside, as an act of inspiration: God fashioned the soul and then "with ˹the knowledge of˺ right and wrong inspired it!" (91:8). Between the external showing of the way and the internal recognition of good and evil, the human being is equipped twice over — once by what is placed before him and once by what is placed within him.

The two ways have a named source. Sufyān ath-Thawrī transmits from ʿĀṣim, from Zirr, from ʻAbdullah bin Masʿud, that the two ways are the good and the evil, and the same sense is recorded from ʿAli, Ibn ʻAbbas, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Abū Waʾil, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Muhammad bin Kaʻ, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī. The unanimity matters, because it fixes what kind of showing this is. The two roads are not two schools of thought or two ways of living; they are the good and the evil, named in the singular and set side by side. It is the same pairing the sūrah of Man gives when it says that humanity was made a hearer and a seer in order to be tried, and that the way was shown to it whether it proved grateful or ungrateful (76:3, quoted above).

**Showing Is Not Compelling**

The verb in this verse is *hadaynāhu*, we guided or showed him, and it is used in a sense that stops short of forcing the outcome. The Qur'an makes the point in the plainest terms where it tells the Prophet that guidance of hearts is not his office: "You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills" (28:56).

**The Universality of the Showing**

The pronoun is general, and the gift is not restricted to a community, a time or a place. The revelation describes the same universal endowment elsewhere in the language of an original disposition: "the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people. Let there be no change in this creation of Allah" (30:30). Read alongside the two ways of this verse, the picture is consistent. Human beings are not born morally blank and then instructed; they are born oriented, and the instruction they receive confirms an orientation already present. That matters for the argument the sūrah is making. Ignorance is not available as a defence to the man who boasts about his wealth.
verses.11:
> If only they had attempted the challenging path ˹of goodness instead˺

**A Sentence That Is Both Wish and Reproach**

*Fa-lā iqtahama al-ʿaqabah* is one of the most compressed lines in the Qur'an. The particle *lā* after *fa* can carry an urging — "would that he charged the pass!" — or a plain negative — "but he did not charge the pass". Both readings are grammatically sound and they converge on the same accusation, because a wish that something had happened is a statement that it did not. The urging reading has the stronger rhetorical effect. It presents the ascent as something still possible, something the hearer can undertake while the sentence is being read, and it registers the loss as a loss rather than as a verdict already sealed. Translations split accordingly: some render the line as a statement of failure, others as a reproachful wish. The difference in tone matters more than the difference in grammar. The verse is not closing a file; it is standing at the foot of a slope asking why nobody has started climbing.

**The Pass Is Defined at Once**

The reproach does not stand alone for even one verse. Ibn Zayd read the line as an urging — will he not charge the pass that holds his safety and his good? — and noted that God explains that pass immediately, by what follows: freeing a neck, or giving food. The sūrah therefore does the opposite of what a rhetorical question usually does. It raises the difficulty and then refuses to leave it undefined, because an ascent nobody can describe can be admired without ever being climbed. What comes next is a definition in the plainest available terms, and it is where the weight of the chapter sits. This verse is the foot of the slope; the description of the climb is given within the next four.
verses.12:
> And what will make you realize what ˹attempting˺ the challenging path is

**A Formula Reserved for Great Things**

*Wa-mā adrāka* is a fixed formula, and the Qur'an deploys it with discipline. It appears where the subject exceeds the hearer's frame of reference and the text intends to enlarge it. Of the Fire described as the Crusher, the verse asks: "And what will make you realize what the Crusher is?" (104:5). Of the abyss that will house those whose scale is light, it asks: "And what will make you realize what that is?" (101:10), and answers, "˹It is˺ a scorching Fire" (101:11). The construction does three things at once: it declares the subject weighty, it admits that the hearer does not yet grasp it, and it prepares him for a definition he could not have produced himself. Its use here tells the reader that what follows is not a footnote to the previous verse but the centre of the sūrah. Everything said so far — the oath, the human condition, the faculties, the two ways — has been leading to a definition the text treats as beyond ordinary expectation.

**Why the Ordinary Answer Is the Real One**

The correction works because it removes an evasion. A moral demand framed as a cosmic ordeal can be admired from a distance; nobody is expected to storm a mountain of judgment, so nobody feels reproached by it. A demand framed as feeding a relative cannot be admired from a distance, because the relative exists and the famine is happening. The sūrah's strategy is to make the good unromantic. It strips the ascent of spectacle and leaves the cost, and the cost is denominated in money, food and time. The same method appears in the answer given to the people of the Fire when they are asked what landed them there: "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor" (74:43–44). Two failures are named, and the second is a failure to feed. The definition of the pass in this chapter belongs to that same economy of concrete acts. The ordinary answer is the real one because the ascent is performed in ordinary life. A reader looking for a heroic act has been given feeding and freeing, and the substitution tells him where the difficulty actually lies. The verse relocates the climb from a mountain to a week.
verses.13:
> It is to free a slave

**The Verified Promise Attached to the Act**

The reward promised for manumission is stated in the same physical terms as the act. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, in the Book of Manumission, transmits from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever frees a Muslim slave, Allah will save every limb of his body from the Fire, limb for limb, as he freed the limbs of the slave. The symmetry is exact — a body given back is answered by a body saved — and the tradition preserves the reasoning of the early community, since the same chapter records ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn freeing a slave upon hearing the report. The verse in this sūrah supplies the moral frame for that promise: manumission is not one charitable option among many but the first item in the definition of the difficult road. The jurists who debated whether manumission or ordinary charity is greater had this ordering in front of them, and the placement of the verse before the feeding verses was cited as evidence for the priority of freeing.

The report has a chain worth naming, and the chain is part of its force. Aḥmad records it from Saʿid bin Marjanah, who heard Abū Hurayrah give it, and al-Bukhārī, Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasaʾi all carry it from the same transmitter. When Saʿid had finished, ʿAli bin al-Husayn asked him outright whether he had really heard it from Abū Hurayrah, and on being told yes, he called for Muṭarrif — the quickest of the boys he owned — and said: go, you are free for the face of Allah. The hearing produced the act in the same hour, which is the shortest distance there is between a text and a practice.

**A Neck Rather Than a Person**

The Arabic is *fakk raqabah*, literally the unloosing of a neck. The choice of the part for the whole is not casual. A neck is where bondage is physically located: the yoke, the collar, the rope. To speak of the neck is to speak of the exact point at which one human being is fastened to another's will. The word also carries the sense of a life — the neck is the seat of the self in Arabic phrase, and *raqabah* can mean the person as a whole. Both senses are present, and both do work. The concrete sense keeps the act physical: there is a bond, and it is undone. The wider sense makes the act total: what is released is not a limb but a life, returned to its own direction. The verse asks for neither a partial manumission nor a kindness within slavery.

**The Same Promise Attached to Other Acts**

Aḥmad preserves a wider list from ʿAmr bin ʻAbasah, in which freeing a person stands beside two other acts: whoever builds a mosque so that Allah may be remembered in it, Allah will build him a house in Paradise; whoever frees a Muslim, it will be his ransom from the Fire; and whoever grows grey in Islam will have his grey hair as a light on the Day of Judgement. A second route, through Abū Umāmah, adds the measure that makes the comparison exact: whoever shoots an arrow in Allah's cause that reaches the enemy, whether it hits or misses, has the reward of freeing a slave. Aḥmad collected these reports through several chains that Ibn Kathīr calls good and strong. Read against this verse the list does two things. It sets manumission inside a company of costly acts, and it shows the standard the arrow is measured against — a shot that reaches the enemy, hit or miss, is reckoned at what freeing a person is worth.

**What the Act Cost in That Economy**

Freeing a slave was not a symbolic gesture. It was the surrender of capital, and in a city whose wealth was partly denominated in people, it reduced the owner's standing as well as his assets. The Qur'an acknowledges the cost and legislates around it: masters are told to make contracts of manumission with those slaves they know to be worthy, and to give them from the wealth God has provided (24:33 — *“And give them some of Allah’s wealth which He has granted you.”*). The same act appears inside the definition of righteousness itself, where the righteous are those "who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives" (2:177). The phrase "cherished wealth" is the operative one. The good that counts is the good that hurts, and no expenditure in that list hurts more than the release of a person whose labour the owner was entitled to command. This verse is therefore the sharpest test the sūrah sets. What the act cost in that economy can be measured, and the measurement is what makes the act significant. A reader who knows what a person was worth as property understands that freeing one was a substantial transfer, and the transfer is the reason the verse treats it as an ascent rather than a courtesy.
verses.14:
> or to give food in times of famine

**The Season Is Part of the Definition**

The verse does not say "give food". It says give food *fī yawmin dhī masghabah*, on a day of hunger, in a season of famine. The specification is the point. Food given in abundance costs little and proves little; food given when supplies are short is given out of the giver's own security. The Qur'an states the principle in the language of attachment: the righteous give "out of their cherished wealth" (2:177), and the measure of a gift is not its size but what its absence will cost the one who gives it. By naming the famine, the verse converts charity from a general disposition into a dated act. There is a day, the day is hard, and the gift is to be made then. A reader cannot satisfy this verse by remembering that he has been generous in comfortable years. The verse asks for the specific occasion on which generosity is most expensive.

The word itself is a language point the early commentators took care to fix. *Masghabah* comes from *saghb*, and Ibn Kathīr gives it plainly as hunger — the gloss Ibn ʻAbbas gave, with ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatādah saying the same. The day named in the verse is therefore not a season in the calendar but a condition in bodies. It is the day on which hunger is the general fact, and the gift is measured against that fact. A reader who supplies his own image of famine — a poor harvest, a rise in prices — has softened the word. What the verse asks for is food given while people are hungry.

**Why Scarcity Multiplies the Gift**

Two things change in a famine, and both increase the weight of what is given. The first is the value of the thing itself. Grain in a year of plenty is a commodity; grain in a year of shortage is survival, and the same measure carries a different meaning. The second is the state of the giver. A man who feeds others while his own store is adequate performs a kindness; a man who does it while his own household is short performs a sacrifice. The revelation names the second case explicitly in its description of the righteous: they "give food—despite their desire for it—to the poor, the orphan, and the captive" (76:8), and the motive is recorded in the next verse as being for God's sake alone, seeking neither reward nor thanks (76:9 — *“˹saying to themselves,˺ “We feed you only for the sake of Allah, seeking neither reward nor thanks from you”*). The phrase "despite their desire for it" is the definition of a famine gift. The giver wants the food, and gives it anyway.

**The Famine Gift Is Best Given Where Nobody Watches**

Scarcity changes the audience as well as the cost. In a famine everyone knows who has stores, and a public distribution buys reputation at the exact moment the giver can least afford the food. The verse does not ask for a display, and the Qur'an is explicit about the ranking: "To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you of your sins. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do" (2:271). Private giving in a season of shortage is the hardest form of the act, because the giver loses both the food and the credit. That is precisely the combination the boastful man at the head of the chapter could not imagine. He needed the audience, and his need for it is what turned his expenditure into a complaint. Feeding in a famine is set against that posture. The verse asks for the transfer of food, not for the announcement of it, and the announcement is worth nothing in the accounting the sūrah has already described.
verses.15:
> to an orphaned relative

**The Orphan's Property Is Protected by the Same Concern**

Feeding an orphaned relative is one half of the duty; the other half is not consuming what he already has. The revelation legislates the second with unusual sharpness: "Do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity" (17:34). The permission granted inside the prohibition is narrow and specific — a guardian may manage the child's property to increase it — and the deadline is fixed. Where the community asks how to deal with orphans, the answer is the same: "Improving their condition is best" (2:220). The sūrah of the Dawn indicts the opposite behaviour in a single line: "And you devour ˹others’˺ inheritance greedily" (89:19). Read against this verse, the picture is complete. The orphaned relative is exposed twice: he needs food because he has no provider, and he holds property that his relatives are positioned to absorb. The chapter asks for the first need to be met, and the wider revelation forbids the second temptation from being acted on.

**Yatīm: A Word With Legal Precision**

*Yatīm* in Arabic means a child who has lost his father, and the majority of the commentators and jurists define it that way, while some extend it to the loss of both parents. The word's legal sense is tied to the loss of the provider rather than to grief as such, and it lapses at maturity: in Islamic law the orphan's special status ends when he reaches adulthood and can manage his own affairs. That precision matters for reading the verse. The person to be fed is not any bereaved person but a child who has lost the one who fed him. The sūrah's other items are equally concrete — a neck to be freed, a poor man in the dust — and this one is no exception. The demand is addressed to a specific situation that a reader can check against his own family: is there a child in your kinship who no longer has a father, and what has your wealth done for him?

**A Concern Repeated Across the Revelation**

The orphan is among the most frequently named recipients of moral attention in the Qur'an, and the repetition is a rebuke rather than a reminder. The sūrah of the Dawn states the failure flatly: "Absolutely not! In fact, you are not ˹even˺ gracious to the orphan" (89:17). The sūrah of Small Kindnesses identifies the denier of the Judgment by his treatment of the child without a father: "That is the one who repulses the orphan" (107:2). The covenant taken from the children of Israel places kindness to orphans next to worship of God and kindness to parents (2:83 — *“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.”*). Read together, these verses describe a society's standing as measurable by a single variable: how it treats children who have lost their provider. This sūrah makes the same measurement, with the added weight of kinship. The orphan who is your relative is the case in which your society's failure and your own failure are the same act. The concern is repeated across the revelation, and the repetition is what establishes it as an obligation rather than a preference. A reader who finds the same instruction in several chapters understands that he is not reading an isolated remark. The consistency is the evidence of its weight.

**The Kinship Doubles the Gift**

The two halves of the verse are worth their separate weights, and the early glosses keep them apart: the orphan is the one who is fed, and "of near relationship" means one who is related to the giver — Ibn ʻAbbas, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and as-Suddī all read it that way. The combination is then paid for twice. Aḥmad records from Salmān bin ʿĀmir that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: charity given to a poor person counts as one charity, while charity given to a relative counts as two — charity, and the keeping of ties. At-Tirmidhī and an-Nasaʾi carry the same report, and its chain is noted as authentic. That is the arithmetic the verse implies without stating it. The nearest claim on a man's food is the child in his own family who has lost a father, and the gift made there does the work of two.

**The Orphan to Whom the Sūrah Was Revealed**

The verse has a biographical resonance for its first hearer. The Prophet ﷺ was an orphan: his father ʿAbdullāh died before he was born, his mother Āmina died when he was about six, and his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib died when he was about eight, leaving him in the household of an uncle. The revelation returns to this repeatedly, and the sūrah of the Morning Light puts it as a question from God: "Did He not find you as an orphan then sheltered you?" (93:6).
verses.16:
> or to a poor person in distress

**The Dust as a Description of Homelessness**

*Dhā matrabah* is literally "possessor of dust", and the commentators gloss it as the man who has no home other than the ground. The image is exact and unsentimental. A person whose bed is dust has lost not only wealth but shelter, privacy and standing; he is visible in public in a state that most people arrange never to be seen in. The Qur'an's use of concrete physical description here does the same work it does elsewhere in the chapter — the neck for bondage, the famine for scarcity, the dust for destitution. Each term fixes the reader's attention on a body rather than on a category. The poor person of this verse is not a statistic in a discussion of poverty. He is a man lying on the ground, and the verse asks whether he was fed. The dust describes homelessness rather than filth, and the reader should hold that sense. A person lying in the dust has no floor, no roof and no place to be, and the verse names the condition by its visible mark. The image is chosen because it cannot be mistaken for anything else.

Ibn ʻAbbas put the picture in a single sentence. *Dhā matrabah*, he said, is the man who is dejected in the street and has no house or anything else to protect him from the dirt. The definition is negative and exact: the man is in the road, and he has nothing between his body and the ground. The whole phrase is given as poor, wretched and clinging to the dirt — destitution rather than a modest income. That is why the verse names the dust at all. Wealth that is merely small still leaves a man a doorway; the dust means he has none.

**Miskīn and Faqīr: A Distinction the Jurists Debated**

Arabic has two words for the needy, and the jurists have argued about their precise relationship. The debate is recorded in the legal literature because both words appear in the verse on zakāh recipients, and the categories determine who qualifies.

What the debate never disturbs is the qualification this verse sets. Both words stand side by side in the list of those entitled to the alms-tax, "Alms-tax is only for the poor and the needy" (9:60 — *“Alms-tax is only for the poor and the needy”*), and the order there has been argued over for the same reason. For a reader of this sūrah the distinction changes nothing. The recipient here is identified not by a category but by a visible condition — he is lying in the dust — and a man in that state qualifies under either name.

**The Man in the Dust Has No One to Speak for Him**

Destitution removes a person's ability to make a claim. A relative can ask; a neighbour can complain; a debtor can be pressed by others on his behalf. The man lying in the dust has none of these, and his need is known only to those who look. The verse addresses that asymmetry directly by making his case a religious obligation rather than a matter of his own advocacy. The Qur'an's concern for the voiceless is consistent across its legislation, and it appears wherever power is uneven: the same chapter that commands kindness to the orphaned relative forbids approaching the orphan's property except to improve it (17:34 — *“Do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity. Honour ˹your˺ pledges, for you will surely be accountable for them”*), because the child cannot defend it. The poor person in distress is in the same position about food.
verses.17:
> and—above all—to be one of those who have faith and urge each other to perseverance and urge each other to compassion

**Faith Stated as the Ground, Not as a Fourth Item**

Three acts of expenditure have been listed, and then a fourth clause is added that is not an act at all. The conjunction joining it — "and" — can be read either as adding another requirement or as attaching a condition to the ones already given. The conditional reading is the one the commentators prefer, and it is the one that makes sense of the sentence. Faith is not a fourth deed standing beside freeing and feeding; it is the state in which those deeds count. The verse says "to be one of those who have faith", using the language of belonging rather than of performing. A person is inside a group, and the group is defined first by belief and then by two forms of mutual encouragement. Everything he does follows from that membership, and without it the deeds have no footing. Stating faith as the ground rather than as a fourth item changes how the list is read. A reader who counts three acts and a belief has misread the structure; the belief is the condition under which the acts count. The verse places it accordingly and the placement is the argument.

**Why the Condition Is Necessary**

The Qur'an states the point directly where it explains the rejection of a people's spending: "And what prevented their donations from being accepted is that they have lost faith in Allah and His Messenger, they never come to prayer except half-heartedly, and they never donate except resentfully" (9:54). The verse names the two symptoms — reluctant prayer and resentful giving — and traces both to a single cause. This is precisely the man quoted at the head of the chapter. He gave, and he resented giving, and his resentment was not a mood but a symptom of what he actually believed.

The gloss on this clause is short and does the structural work: then, along with these beautiful and pure characteristics, he was a believer in his heart, seeking the reward of that from Allah. The two conditions are belief and intention, and the revelation states them as plainly as this verse does (17:19 — *“But whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it accordingly, and is a ˹true˺ believer, it is they whose striving will be appreciated”*). The same condition is attached to good work in the sūrah of the Bee (16:97 — *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer”*). This verse says it by word order alone, putting belief first in the sentence.

**Urging One Another to Perseverance**

The first of the two reciprocal acts is urging to patience, and the Qur'an's shortest chapter makes it one of the four marks of those who escape ruin: "except those who have faith, do good, and urge each other to the truth, and urge each other to perseverance" (103:3). Patience here is not passive endurance but sustained practice under opposition.

The gloss for this half of the clause is specific about what the patience is for. The believers of this verse, Ibn Kathīr says, advised one another to be patient with the harm people do them, and to be merciful to them. Patience is therefore not a private temperament but a counsel passed between people, and its object is the injury other human beings cause. That is the patience this sūrah has been describing from its first verse: the man abused in his own city, the orphan passed by, the beggar left in the road. Urging it on one another is how a community keeps it possible at all.

**Urging One Another to Compassion**

The second reciprocal act is urging to mercy, and it is distinct from the first. The pairing covers both axes of the moral life, and the Qur'an grounds the second in the purpose of the revelation itself: "We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world" (21:107).

Three reports on mercy are attached to the second half of the clause. In the first, the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: the merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful; be merciful to those on earth and the One above the heavens will be merciful to you. The second states it as a refusal: Allah will not be merciful to whoever is not merciful to people. The third narrows the mercy to a household and a street. Abū Dāwūd records from ʻAbdullah bin ʿAmr that the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever does not show mercy to our young, and does not recognise the right of our elders, is not of us. That last phrase is the sharpest of the three. Mercy here is not a mood but a test of membership, and it is applied at the two ends of a community — the child who cannot ask, and the elder who should not have to. The verse asks believers to urge this mercy on one another, which is why the urging matters as much as the feeling.
verses.18:
> These are the people of the right

**The Right Hand and What It Holds**

The imagery of right and left in the Qur'an is tied to the record of deeds and to the hand in which it is received. "As for those who are given their record in their right hand" (84:7) introduces a scene of relief; the same scene appears in the sūrah of the Inevitable, where the one given his record in his right hand cries out happily, "Here ˹everyone˺! Read my record!" (69:19). The Day of Summoning is described in the same terms: "whoever will be given their record in their right hand will read it ˹happily˺ and will not be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone" (17:71). The right hand is therefore not an abstract symbol of favour but a specific moment: the receipt of one's own account, in public, without shame. The people of this verse are the people who can look at what they did. That is the meaning the sūrah has been building toward, since the acts it lists were all performed where other people could see them or not.

**A Company, Not a List of Individuals**

The word used is *aṣḥāb*, companions or people of, and it means a group held together by a shared attribute. The plural is not incidental. The acts described in the previous verses were individual — a man frees a slave, a household feeds a relative — but the final urging was reciprocal, and the title reflects that reciprocity. The people of the right are a company. They are described elsewhere in the same collective terms: "the people of the right, how ˹blessed˺ will they be" (56:8), and "And the people of the right—how ˹blessed˺ will they be!" (56:27). The exclamation in those verses belongs to a scene of arrival, and it is addressed to the group rather than to any member of it. This sūrah uses the same title without the exclamation, which leaves the emphasis on the qualification rather than on the celebration. A company rather than a list of individuals is what the term means, and the difference matters. A reader who reads the verse as naming particular people has narrowed it; the description fits anyone who meets the conditions, and the openness is what allows him to place himself in it.

**The Record Can Be Read in Public Without Shame**

The title of this group points to a moment of exposure. The record of deeds will be laid open, and the scene is described without mercy for the wicked: "They will cry, ‘Woe to us! What kind of record is this that does not leave any sin, small or large, unlisted?’ They will find whatever they did present ˹before them˺" (18:49). Nothing is omitted, and the omission of nothing is exactly what makes the moment bearable for one group and unbearable for the other. The people of the right are the ones who can be handed their own account in front of witnesses and read it, because the entries in it were made deliberately: a person freed, a relative fed, a stranger in the dust given food, patience and mercy urged on others. The verse's short verdict is therefore a statement about visibility. What these people did, they did where it could be seen, and the seeing does not undo it.
verses.19:
> As for those who deny Our signs, they are the people of the left

**Denial of the Signs Is the Specific Charge**

The charge is *kafarū bi-āyātinā* — they disbelieved in Our signs — and the signs have been on display since the first verse. The city sworn by is a sign. The faculties listed, the eyes and the tongue and the lips, are signs. The two ways shown to humanity are signs. The verse therefore does not accuse this group of ignorance but of refusal. They were shown, and they denied what was shown. That distinction matters, because it removes the defence of incomprehension. The signs in this chapter are not obscure propositions; they are the reader's own eyes and the road in front of him. Denial of them is not an intellectual position but a decision, and the verse treats it as one. Denial of the signs is the specific charge, and the specificity matters. A reader who assumes the charge is general wrongdoing has widened it; the verse names a particular refusal, and the naming allows him to check whether the refusal is present in himself.

**The People of the Left Described Elsewhere**

The title given here is expanded in the sūrah of the Event, where the two groups are announced and then described: "the people of the left, how ˹miserable˺ will they be" (56:9), and again "And the people of the left—how ˹miserable˺ will they be!" (56:41). The description that follows is physical and unremitting — scorching heat, boiling water, the shade of black smoke, "neither cool nor refreshing" (56:42–44). The contrast with the people of the right is drawn in the same chapter and in the same terms. This sūrah borrows the title without borrowing the description, which keeps the emphasis where the chapter has placed it throughout: on the acts and their rejection rather than on the scenery of the outcome. The reader is expected to know the rest, and the reference is enough.

**The Signs Were Local Before They Were Universal**

The denial charged in this verse begins at home. The first sign this chapter swears by is the city itself, and the city's status is a fact the deniers lived inside. Their own objection to following the Prophet was economic, and the answer to it is a reminder of the sign they already enjoyed: "Have We not established for them a safe haven ˹in Mecca˺ to which fruits of all kinds are brought as a provision from Us? But most of them do not know ˹this favour˺" (28:57). The final clause states the denial precisely. It is not that the favour was hidden but that it was not recognised. A safe haven in a region of raiding, fruit carried into a waterless valley, custodianship of a House that drew pilgrims from every direction — each of these is a sign, and each was refused by the people who benefited most from it. The verse classifies that refusal, and it does so in the plainest available terms.
verses.20:
> The Fire will be sealed over them

**One Word Carries the Whole Verse**

The chapter ends with a single image, and the image is closure. *Muʾṣadah* describes something shut fast, its doors closed and secured from the outside. The Qur'an uses the same word in the sūrah of the Slanderer, where the Fire is described as sealed over its inhabitants and "˹tightly secured˺ with long braces" (104:8–9). The addition of the braces in that parallel tells the reader what this verse leaves implicit: the sealing is not a temporary measure that might be reversed but a fastening. The brevity of the verse is part of its effect. After twenty verses of oath, argument and definition, the last line is four words long and contains no qualification, no explanation and no offer. The chapter ends where its argument ends, and it ends shut. One word carries the whole verse, and the reader who understands the word understands the chapter's ending. The term describes a closure that is final rather than temporary, and the finality is what gives the last verse its weight. The verse is brief because the word is enough.

The word's meaning is not in dispute among the early authorities, and the list of those who glossed it is long: Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʻAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Mujāhid, Muhammad bin Kaʻ al-Quraẓī, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī all gave it as shut. Ibn ʻAbbas said its doors will be closed. Ad-Dahhak added the detail that there will be no door at all — sealed over them, with no door. Qatādah filled in the rest of the picture: it will be shut, and there will be no light in it, no crack, and no way out of it, forever. Three glosses, and between them they take away every escape the word might have allowed. A door can be opened; a wall with no door cannot. A sealed room can hold a crack of light; this one holds none.

**The Sanctuary's Doors and the Fire's Doors**

The chapter opened by swearing on a city whose defining feature was access. The Sacred House was made "a centre and a sanctuary for the people", a place for those who circle it, meditate in it, bow and prostrate (2:125 — *“And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.”*), and its residents were fed and kept safe so that worship could continue (106:4 — *“Who has fed them against hunger and made them secure against fear”*). Doors in that city were open by design: pilgrims came, traders came, and the House existed to be approached. The last verse of the chapter describes the opposite kind of door. The Fire is sealed over its inhabitants, fastened from outside, with no approach and no departure. The contrast between the two doors is the chapter's final image, and it is not accidental. A city built for approach ends by producing, for some of its residents, a place that cannot be approached or left. What decides which door a person meets is the conduct described in the middle of the chapter.

**Withholding Food and Meeting Fire**

The punishment described in the closing verses answers the offences described in the middle ones. The man who complained about the wealth he had spent refused to feed; the sūrah of the Clothed One records the confession of those in the Fire, "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor" (74:43–44). The correspondence is exact, and it is the same in this chapter. Food was withheld in a famine, the orphaned relative was passed by, the man in the dust was left where he lay, and a neck stayed bound. The Fire is then described in what those people refused to give: no relief, no air, no exit, and no lightening of the punishment (43:75 — *“It will never be lightened for them, and there they will be overwhelmed with despair”*). Every refusal recorded earlier in the chapter has a shape, and the shape of the ending is the same shape turned around.
